title: From Amritsar's Streets to TIME100: Vikas Khanna's Journey to Global Culinary Stardom
excerpt: Born with clubfoot and bullied as a child, the Michelin-starred chef built a culinary empire in New York, earned a TIME100 honor in 2026, and is now redefining Indian cuisine on the world stage through his restaurant Bungalow.
body:
• Vikas Khanna, born in Amritsar with clubfoot, overcame childhood bullying and homelessness in New York to become a Michelin-starred chef, MasterChef India judge, and author of over 35 books.
  • He was named to the TIME100 list of the world's most influential people in 2026, profiled by chef Eric Ripert as "a man of extraordinary heart."
  • His New York restaurant Bungalow, a tribute to his late sister Radhika, had 100,000 people on its waitlist during Ramzan 2026 and has become a cultural institution.
  • During the pandemic, Khanna's Feed India initiative served over 50 million meals across the country.

A Kitchen Born of Adversity

When Vikas Khanna was born in Amritsar in 1971, doctors told his mother, Bindu Khanna, that her son's feet were deformed and he might never walk or run. She refused to accept the diagnosis. "My son is not born to walk, he is born to fly," she told them, taking him to Delhi for further treatment.

Khanna grew up wearing leg braces and wooden shoes, enduring relentless bullying from classmates who called him "polio wala ladka." He found refuge in two kitchens: his grandmother's, where he learned the foundations of Indian cooking, and the Golden Temple's langar in Amritsar, where he assisted in the community kitchen that feeds thousands daily.

By 13, he was helping his mother sell chole bhature outside a local school. He became the sous chef in his mother's banquet business, Lawrence Garden, operating out of the family home. When local authorities demolished the banquet operation a decade later, Khanna left for New York with almost nothing.

31 Jobs and a Michelin Star

New York was unsparing. Khanna took on 31 odd jobs — washing dishes, cleaning homes, working in delis and cafes, looking after pets. He sold food on the streets of TriBeCa, slept at Grand Central Terminal, and spent nights in homeless shelters. On the subway, strangers called him "Curry Boy." While working in a restaurant in Paris, a chef told him, "Black hands don't cook, they only clean." He quit on the spot.

In 2010, Khanna returned to New York and opened Junoon in Manhattan. The restaurant earned a Michelin star the following year, making him one of the few Indian chefs in the Western world to achieve the distinction. He went on to host multiple seasons of MasterChef India, authored more than 35 books — including the 1,200-page culinary opus Utsav — and personally delivered copies to Queen Elizabeth, President Barack Obama, and Pope Francis.

"People can take everything from you, but not your pride and happiness."

— Vikas Khanna

Bungalow: A Sister's Dream Realized

Khanna's older sister Radhika, a fashion designer who lived for years with lupus, pushed him to rethink his approach to food. She told him his Michelin-era cooking had lost its identity — that he had forgotten who he was cooking for. His mother delivered a similar verdict after visiting Junoon: "Yeh toh khaana humare country ka nahi hai. Whose food is this?"

From her hospital bed, Radhika kept designing a restaurant with him — the carvings on the walls, the vision of crowds lining the block, nine straight days of Durga Pooja. She texted him décor ideas until she died in his arms in 2022. Parcels she had ordered kept arriving in New York under her name.

Bungalow, which opened in New York's East Village in 2024, is that restaurant. Its reservations sold out in 11 seconds. During Ramzan 2026, 100,000 people were on the waitlist. There are bhangra dancers at 4 p.m. and nine-day Durga Pooja celebrations. It is unapologetically Indian in a way Junoon never was.

TIME100 and a Larger Mission

In April 2026, Khanna was named to the TIME100 list of the world's most influential people, profiled by chef Eric Ripert, who called him "a man of extraordinary heart." Khanna, now 54, said the recognition holds particular weight in the culinary world. "If your name comes in the Michelin guide, then also you're hoping you get featured in TIME magazine. This is the peak," he told Esquire India.

Beyond the kitchen, Khanna's Feed India initiative distributed over 50 million meals during the pandemic. His film The Last Color, inspired by the isolation of Indian widows during Holi, screened at over 100 festivals and led to his appointment as global ambassador for the Global Fund for Widows.

"She made me realise that you think wearing the Michelin crown on your head is the peak. But it's not."

— Vikas Khanna, on his sister Radhika's influence

When the TIME100 news broke, the first person Khanna called was his mother. "Mera toh koi rishtedaar padh nahi raha TIME magazine Amritsar mein," he said — none of my relatives in Amritsar are reading TIME magazine. The second message came from Priyanka Chopra. Shah Rukh Khan once told him his food tasted like home, a compliment Khanna says he has never forgotten.

"This validation has come at a very different time," Khanna said, "when I'm not seeking any validation or any fame or awards, but I'm grateful."
nri_angle: Khanna's journey from Amritsar to Michelin stardom and the TIME100 list embodies the Indian diaspora experience of overcoming adversity abroad while staying rooted in Indian identity and culture.
author: Diaspora Desk
